title: Will we reach peak oil?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss peak oil: the point at which global oil production plateaus and begins to decline while demand keeps rising. They explain that oil is a finite, non-renewable resource, the difference between peak oil and running out, and the debate between peak oil adherents and optimists such as the Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA). They cover BP Statistical Review reserve figures (1.2 trillion barrels in 2008, 1.6 trillion in 2012), M. King Hubbert's 1950s curve and his prediction about US production, the three-stage oil extraction process and why some oil (Arctic, deep ocean, oil shale, tar sands) remains untapped, US oil imports and consumption trends, alternative fuels and natural gas, coal-to-liquid fuel, the Hirsch Report's mitigation scenarios, and the 2008 oil price peak. The episode closes with listener mail from Eric Stephens about supporting local orchestras.

segments.title: Opening banter and election day
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joke about the episode's release timing and election day, and set up the topic of peak oil.

segments.title: What peak oil is and why it will happen
segments.summary: Peak oil is defined as the point when oil production can no longer keep up with demand, not when oil runs out. Oil is a finite, non-renewable fossil fuel that takes millions of years to form. Experts broadly agree the peak will come, though debate continues over timing and aftermath.

segments.title: M. King Hubbert and the Hubbert curve
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Hubbert curve, in which production from a reserve rises, plateaus, and declines. Hubbert predicted US peak production in the early 1970s, missing by about a year, and US production peaked and has declined since.

segments.title: Proved reserves and BP's statistics
segments.summary: BP's Statistical Review reported proved reserves of 1.2 trillion barrels in 2008 and 1.6 trillion in 2012. The hosts explain what proved reserves mean and why reserve figures may be unreliable since reporters are not audited.

segments.title: Optimists versus peak oil adherents and the relay race analogy
segments.summary: CERA argued there was ample oil, citing about 3.74 trillion barrels and an undulating plateau. BP's figure implies about 54 years of reserves. The hosts compare the situation to a relay race, with consumption, production, and alternative fuels as runners. Changing CAFE standards and growing demand in China and India affect the outcome.

segments.title: Oil imports, consumption, and transportation use
segments.summary: About 70 percent of US petroleum goes to transportation. US oil consumption and imports have declined, with imports reaching a twenty-year low in 2012 even though the share of imports was about 60 percent in 2011. Natural gas and new domestic finds are also rising.

segments.title: Extraction stages, untapped oil, and alternative fuels
segments.summary: Primary extraction yields about ten percent of a reservoir, secondary recovery with CO2 or water adds more, and remaining oil in the Arctic, deep ocean, oil shale, and tar sands stays untapped because it is expensive. The hosts discuss alternative fuels, switchgrass and ethanol, liquid coal, and the Hirsch Report's mitigation scenarios.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh reads listener mail from Eric Stephens, a double bass player in Germany, praising classical music and urging listeners to support local orchestras. The hosts close with contact information.
